svg.data-vd-play-label: Play: four ways substances cross the membrane
svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Simple diffusion: small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen pass straight through the phospholipid bilayer, from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated. No energy is needed."], [5, "Facilitated diffusion: ions and large polar molecules cannot cross the bilayer, so they diffuse through channel proteins or are carried by carrier proteins that change shape. Still down the gradient, and no ATP."], [10, "Osmosis: water molecules move from the dilute solution (higher water potential) to the concentrated solution (lower water potential). The solute molecules are too big to pass: the membrane is partially permeable."], [15, "Active transport: a carrier protein uses energy from ATP to move ions from a lower to a higher concentration, against the concentration gradient. Cells that do a lot of it have many mitochondria."]]
svg.title: Transport across the cell membrane
svg.desc: A phospholipid bilayer with simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion through a channel and a carrier protein, osmosis through an aquaporin, and active transport by a pump using ATP.
svg.text: How substances cross the cell membrane
The dots show concentration: more dots, higher concentration. Not to scale.

g.data-info: Tissue fluid or the surrounding solution.
Two layers of phospholipids: hydrophilic heads facing the water on each side, hydrophobic tails inside. Small non-polar molecules pass through it; ions and large polar molecules cannot.

Net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, directly through the bilayer. Passive: no energy from respiration. Example: oxygen and carbon dioxide in gas exchange.
A protein with a water-filled pore that lets specific ions diffuse through (facilitated diffusion). Some open and close (gated).
Binds a specific molecule (here glucose), changes shape and releases it on the other side. Facilitated diffusion: down the gradient, no ATP.
Net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (higher water potential) to a more concentrated solution (lower water potential) across a partially permeable membrane.
A channel protein for water that speeds up osmosis.
Active transport: moves particles against their concentration gradient, from low to high concentration, using energy released from ATP made in respiration.

g.text: 1 Simple diffusion: through the bilayer, high → low
2 Facilitated diffusion: channel and carrier proteins, high → low
3 Osmosis: water to the lower water potential
4 Active transport: low → high, using ATP
